newsitem.title: USA: Clinton in frenetic election-eve get-out-the-vote drive.
newsitem.headline: Clinton in frenetic election-eve get-out-the-vote drive.

text.p: Giddy with nervous excitement and bleary-eyed from lack of sleep, President Bill Clinton spent the final hours before Tuesday's election trying to make sure his supporters go to the polls.

Clinton campaigned along the eastern seaboard Sunday, jetstopping from sunny Florida to frosty Maine and ending up well after midnight with an airport rally in Bangor. As he walked to the plane after the rally, he said, "It's going to be a good last day."
Everywhere he went, his appeal was the same: for reconciliation, unity and votes.

"This is an election of enormous moment," he told more than 20,000 people who turned out to cheer him in Springfield, Massachusetts. "I want us to do more together. It takes a village to raise a child and build a country and create a future."

His mention of his wife Hillary's book about child-rearing, "It Takes a Village," drew sustained applause, signalling the crowd's disapproval of Republican criticism of his controversial, activist spouse.

The stop in Massachusetts, where some polls show Clinton leading Dole by as much as 30 percentage points, was intended to boost the chances of Democratic Sen. John Kerry. Kerry is locked in a neck-and-neck struggle for re-election with popular Massachusetts Republican Gov. William Weld.

Clinton's election-eve stumping on Monday was to start with a visit to the Merrimack Restaurant in Manchester where John Kennedy, the president's boyhood idol, launched his campaign for the White House in 1960.

He then planned to travel to Cleveland for a noontime rally with Vice President Al Gore that was designed to counter a late surge in Ohio by Republican Bob Dole. Hillary Rodham Clinton and Tipper Gore were also to speak at the rally.
After Cleveland, Clinton was to hopscotch by air across the Midwest, stopping in Lexington, Kentucky, Des Moines, Iowa, and Sioux Falls, South Dakota, before flying home to Little Rock, Arkansas.

The Clinton camp was confident of victory in Tuesday's election, and the mood aboard the president's plane was euphoric, like a winning team's locker room. Clinton aides predicted he would defeat Dole in every one of the states on the final swing, and said he was only going to two of them -- Iowa and South Dakota -- to help Democratic candidates for the Senate.

Although polling conducted for Reuters shows Clinton's lead over Dole narrowing, Clinton campaign officials insisted their extensive polling showed the incumbent with a steady 12 to 15 percentage point lead.
A New York Times/CBS News poll released Monday put Clinton's lead at 16 points over Dole, the same margin he had a year ago.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton had already set in motion a process to review potential staff changes if he is re-elected. He said Clinton would move quickly to reshape his team, including Cabinet officers.

Officials said there were no plans for a huge administration shakeup, although several key Clinton aides were expected to leave. White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta has said he plans to step down, perhaps to run for California governor.
